name: Tulpa creation

lead: A tulpa is an imagined companion that practitioners try to develop through sustained attention, visualisation and conversation, until it feels like it thinks and responds independently. The term comes from the Tibetan sprul pa and was reshaped by Western theosophists and then by online communities.

In looksmaxxing spaces the practice is discussed as a mental skill that may support confidence and company, not as a physical change. Any appearance payoff would come through mood and social comfort, and members mostly share written guides.

paras: Guides describe drafting a profile of the companion's personality, then repeating focused imagery and conversation over weeks, treating the companion as a stream of thought to be filtered and strengthened. Results are described as varying widely.

A 2016 survey found higher rates of autism and ADHD among tulpa practitioners than the general population and suggested loneliness may motivate some. A 2022 study linked the practice to hallucination proneness in people without psychosis. Practitioners in one survey mostly reported improved mental condition.

lead: A tulpa is an imagined companion that practitioners develop deliberately, treating it as sapient and relatively autonomous [1]. The word comes from the Tibetan sprul pa, which may mean phantom, and the modern practice (tulpamancy) grew in online communities on 4chan and Reddit [1].

On looksmax.org the practice appears as a guide framing tulpa creation as filtering, strengthening and refining thought streams that already exist rather than creating something from nothing [2]. It sits in the fringe corner of the forum rather than in appearance advice.
Research on the community is limited to surveys and small studies, described below [1].

paras: Wikipedia traces the term to Tibetan Buddhism, notes that Western ideas of tulpas developed separately through European mystical writers, and says theosophists in the twentieth century merged tulku and thoughtform concepts; Annie Besant's 1905 Thought-Forms and Alexandra David-Néel's account of creating a monk-shaped tulpa are the usual references [1]. The modern willed-imaginary-friend meaning formed in online communities, which are small, with low hundreds of active members each [1].

Practitioners regard tulpas as sapient and relatively autonomous, and some report communication that feels external to their own thoughts or hallucinations in sight, sound or touch [1]. A looksmax.org guide advises building a blueprint of the companion's personality traits before starting and releasing anxiety about timeframes [2]. Most practitioners view tulpas as psychological rather than paranormal [1].

Wikipedia summarises a 2016 survey of 141 tulpamancers by Samuel Veissière that found higher autism and ADHD rates than the general population and suggested loneliness as motivation; in one survey, 93.7 percent said the practice improved their mental condition [1]. A 2022 study linked tulpamancy and ASMR to greater hallucination proneness in people without psychosis, and a 2021 study connected the subculture to reality shifting as a way to cope with loneliness [1].
No studies found. Survey-based research on the community is described above [1].
